content.theory:
Typography defines the voice of your page. Good **font choices** and **spacing** make content effortless to read; bad ones make even great copy feel amateur. The core tool is the **font-family stack** — a comma-separated list the browser walks down until it finds a font that is actually installed on the machine:

```css
body {
  font-family: 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;
}
```
If the user is on Windows they get Segoe UI; on Android the browser falls through to Roboto; on anything else it ends at Arial or the generic `sans-serif`. Always end a stack with a generic family (`serif`, `sans-serif`, `monospace`) so the browser always has a final answer.

### font-size units
`px` is absolute — it ignores the user's browser zoom and font-size preferences. `em` is relative to the **parent** element's font size, which compounds: a `1.5em` element inside a `1.5em` element is effectively `2.25em` of the root. `rem` is relative to the **root** element (`<html>`, default 16px), so it is predictable at every nesting depth:

| Unit | Relative to | Gotcha |
|------|------------|--------|
| px | nothing | ignores browser zoom preferences |
| em | the parent | compounds with nesting |
| rem | the root element | stable and predictable |

Rule of thumb: `px` for borders, `rem` for font sizes and spacing.

### line-height & letter-spacing
`line-height` sets the vertical rhythm of a paragraph — `1.5–1.7` is the comfortable reading range for body text. Set it as a **unitless number** so it scales automatically with whatever font-size the text inherits. `letter-spacing` adds air between characters; `0.5px` on headings or `2px` on uppercase labels is a common designer trick for a premium feel.

### font-weight & web fonts
`font-weight` runs from `100` (thin) to `900` (black); `400` is normal and `700` bold. Browsers *synthesize* missing weights by faux-bolding, which looks bad — better to load real weights, e.g. from Google Fonts:

```css
@import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter:wght@400;600&display=swap');
```
`@import` must be the very first rule in the stylesheet. A `<link>` tag in the `<head>` is faster because it does not block parsing as long, so prefer `<link>` in production.

### text-align
`text-align: left/center/right/justify` controls how lines sit inside their box. `justify` stretches every line to full width and can create ugly "rivers" of white space in narrow columns — reserve it for print. Center-align short headings, but keep body copy left-aligned: centered paragraphs are hard to scan.

Common mistakes: mixing `em` in deeply nested components (the compounding surprise), forgetting the generic family at the end of a stack, and setting `line-height` in `px` so it never scales. Build your type scale in `rem` from the start — it survives zoom, accessibility settings, and responsive breakpoints without rewrites.

exercise.starterCode:
Why Typography Matters

Typography is 90% of web design. The right font stack, size, and spacing turn a block of text into something people actually want to read. Reading comfort comes from rhythm, not decoration.

Notice how this second paragraph inherits the same styling — a well-built type system scales without extra work.
hints: Hint 2: .prose { font-family: 'Georgia', 'Times New Roman', serif; font-size: 1.25rem; line-height: 1.6; letter-spacing: 0.5px; }
Hint 3: 1.25rem = 20px at the default 16px root — try changing it to feel the difference.

rem is relative to the root element, so it stays predictable at any depth
